interest: This file provides valuable insight into both pre-war structural analyses and wartime economic intelligence gathering regarding Japan's agrarian economy. It illustrates how the U.S. State Department tracked Japanese food vulnerabilities, transitioning from pre-Pearl Harbor academic assessments of severe land scarcity and high tenancy rates to mid-war intelligence cables monitoring domestic crop shortages and rationing from neutral Switzerland. The documents are particularly useful for economic historians studying Japanese wartime mobilization, revealing official government attempts to mitigate food crises through state-run monopolies, price incentives, and forced crop substitution from rice to potatoes and hardy grains.
overview: Decimal file 894.61 (spanning April 1941 through June 1944) comprises U.S. diplomatic reporting, research memoranda, and wartime economic intelligence concerning Japanese agriculture, rural economics, and food supply policies before and during World War II. The pre-war documentation includes consular dispatches from Shanghai on Japanese government monopolies over vegetable oils and Manchurian soybeans, as well as Division of Far Eastern Affairs analyses of Dr. Shiroshi Nasu's landmark monograph 'Aspects of Japanese Agriculture', highlighting extreme land scarcity, tenant farming, and rural poverty. The wartime records consist of intelligence cables dispatched from the U.S. Legation in Bern, Switzerland, monitoring Axis press reports and Tokyo broadcasts to assess Japan's deteriorating food situation, diminished rice harvests, and emergency state initiatives promoting the cultivation of substitute staples such as potatoes, wheat, and barley.

subfiles.about: Transmittal of a supplementary memorandum on Japanese vegetable oil control regulations to accompany an annual agricultural policy report.
subfiles.from: Frank P. Lockhart, American Consul General, Shanghai
subfiles.summary: American Consul General Frank P. Lockhart in Shanghai forwards a supplementary memorandum prepared by the Agricultural Attaché regarding the control of vegetable oils and materials in Japan. Lockhart explains that this subject was omitted from the earlier annual report on agricultural policy and programs for the Japanese Empire and occupied territories in China and Manchukuo. He notes that an appendix on furs and skins was compiled by Consul F. W. Hinke and indicates that a further report on Chinese Government agricultural programs in unoccupied China is being prepared.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 408 from Shanghai transmitting supplement on Japanese agricultural policy

subfiles.about: Summary of Japanese imperial ordinances establishing state control companies for the purchase, importation, and distribution of soybeans and vegetable oils.
subfiles.from: Agricultural Attaché, American Consulate General, Shanghai
subfiles.summary: This memorandum details two Japanese control ordinances promulgated in November 1940 governing soybeans, soybean oil, and general vegetable oils and seeds. Under these measures, designated state-controlled corporations obtained monopoly rights over the purchase, importation, and marketing of domestic and Manchurian produce. Importers and manufacturers were required to sell all products to these control companies at government-fixed prices and were prohibited from obtaining raw materials from other sources.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Control of Vegetable Oil in Japan
subfiles.to: Frank P. Lockhart, American Consul General, Shanghai

subfiles.about: Detailed review and statistical extraction of data on land tenure, tenancy, and farm income from Dr. Shiroshi Nasu's monograph.
subfiles.from: Cabot Coville, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Cabot Coville analyzes Dr. Shiroshi Nasu's study, 'Aspects of Japanese Agriculture', prepared for the Institute of Pacific Relations. Coville highlights key findings, including projected population growth leveling off in thirty years, the prevalence of dwarf farms where three-quarters of landowners possessed under 2.5 acres, and a tenant-farming rate of 46.5 percent. The memorandum also compares Japan's cultivated land per worker to that of the United States and cites figures on meager daily farm labor earnings and net agricultural income.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by Cabot Coville reviewing Shiroshi Nasu's 'Aspects of Japanese Agriculture'
subfiles.to: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Adviser on Political Relations

subfiles.about: Routing slip requesting that the Division of Far Eastern Affairs review Dr. Shiroshi Nasu's study for information of interest.
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Adviser on Political Relations
subfiles.summary: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Adviser on Political Relations, refers a copy of Shiroshi Nasu's study to the Division of Far Eastern Affairs. He requests that an officer examine the publication to determine if it contains material of particular interest to the division or himself. This inquiry prompted the detailed statistical summary subsequently prepared by Cabot Coville.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from Stanley K. Hornbeck requesting review of Nasu's study

subfiles.about: Formal acknowledgment of receipt of a complimentary copy of Shiroshi Nasu's monograph from the Institute of Pacific Relations.
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Adviser on Political Relations
subfiles.summary: Stanley K. Hornbeck acknowledges receipt of a copy of 'Aspects of Japanese Agriculture' by Shiroshi Nasu, sent with the compliments of the Research Secretary of the Institute of Pacific Relations in New York. Hornbeck conveys thanks and appreciation on behalf of the Department of State. A true copy of the signed letter was placed in the Department's decimal central files.
subfiles.title: Letter from Stanley K. Hornbeck to the Institute of Pacific Relations

subfiles.about: Intelligence report from Japanese publications detailing food shortages, crop shift initiatives, and agricultural quotas for 1943-1944.
subfiles.from: Leland Harrison, U.S. Minister to Switzerland, Bern
subfiles.summary: Minister Leland Harrison reports data from Japanese publications revealing a deteriorating domestic food situation between 1941 and 1943 caused primarily by adverse weather and lower rice yields. To alleviate shortages, Japanese authorities initiated an intensive shift toward high-yield substitute crops, including sweet potatoes, white potatoes, wheat, barley, and rye. Harrison outlines production figures for 1943 and targeted expansions for 1944, noting substantial official purchase price increases enacted to encourage peasant production and lessen reliance on imported rice.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1995 from Bern on Japanese food situation and crop planning

subfiles.about: Intelligence cable relaying a Tokyo broadcast estimating that the 1944 European potato harvest fell short of wartime targets.
subfiles.from: Leland Harrison, U.S. Minister to Switzerland, Bern
subfiles.summary: Harrison transmits a follow-up intelligence report citing a June 18 Tokyo dispatch regarding the current Japanese European (white) potato crop. The yield was estimated at 720 million kan, an increase over the 540 million kan harvested in 1943, but still well below the government's planned quota. The report notes that harvesting was already completed in Kyushu, Shikoku, and southern islands, and that urban home gardens might augment the final total.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 3959 from Bern on Japanese European potato crop estimates

subfiles.about: Intelligence report citing German press coverage of Japanese wheat and barley crop estimates for 1944.
subfiles.from: Leland Harrison, U.S. Minister to Switzerland, Bern
subfiles.summary: Minister Leland Harrison relays German press reporting from June 17 estimating the 1944 Japanese wheat and barley harvest at 27 million koku. The favorable harvest was attributed to good weather, additional fertilizer allocations, and an increase in sown acreage from 1,683,000 to 1,913,000 cho. The telegram was routed through the Division of Far Eastern Affairs and filed under decimal file 894.61.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 3947 from Bern on Japanese wheat and barley crop estimates
